The universal paper workflow

  1. Circle the deliverable. “ER model,” “candidate keys,” “normalize,” “relational algebra,” and “SQL” demand different output languages.
  2. Write the smallest useful schema. List relation names, keys, and join paths before drawing or querying.
  3. Execute mechanically. Use the recipe beside each worked solution; do not improvise notation under time pressure.
  4. Run the invariant check. Cardinalities, closure, loss of zero rows, grouping grain, and requested sorting catch most errors.
  5. Box the requested result. A marker should find the final relation, SQL statement, or conclusion immediately.

Drill lab: from zero to the answer

Every exam question type, worked on a real exercise. Each drill: the basics in plain words → the real exercise → what to look at → exactly what to write → why it works.

Read this chapter first. The later chapters are the reference; this one is the training. Nothing here assumes you already know the vocabulary—each drill starts by building it.

How each drill is laid outFoundation — the handful of ideas you must own, in everyday language. The exercise — the actual page from the course. What to look at — how to read the prompt and decide what it wants. Write this — the short answer you would actually put on the exam sheet. Why — the full explanation, so the short answer stops being magic.

DRILL 1Draw an ER model from a written description

🔴 Exam-core Prof. Scholz explicitly named ERM as a focus on 22 July 2026; it is drilled in Homework 03, Learning Labs 03–05, and Wrap-Up Task 1.

Foundation — four shapes, that is the whole language

An ER model is a picture of what the database will store, drawn before any table exists. Chen notation uses exactly four things:

  • Rectangle = entity. A thing you will keep many of, each one separately identifiable. Hotel, Room, Guest, Employee. Rule of thumb: it will become a table.
  • Oval = attribute. A fact about one entity. Name, Birthday, Price. It will become a column. Underline the one that identifies the row (the ID) — that is the key.
  • Diamond = relationship. A fact that connects two entities. Hotel includes Room. Employee works for Department. Name it with a verb.
  • Numbers on the lines = cardinality. How many of the other side may each one have. Written 1 or N (or M) at each end.

How to read cardinality without confusing yourself. Always ask the question twice, once from each side, and write the answer at the far end:

"One company has how many departments?" → many → put N at the Department end "One department belongs to how many companies?" → one → put 1 at the Company end result: Company --1-- (consists of) --N-- Department

If both answers are “many”, it is M:N and you will later need a third table. If both are “one”, it is 1:1 and is rare. Most links are 1:N.

What to look at in this prompt
  1. Underline every noun. company, department, employee, producer, retailer → these are candidate entities.
  2. Underline every “is described by / has”. Whatever follows is an attribute. “described by a company ID, a name and a legal form” → three ovals on Company, ID underlined.
  3. Circle every verb between two nouns. “consists of”, “is assigned to”, “is the boss of”, “is head of” → these become diamonds.
  4. Hunt for the counting words. “exactly one”, “one to many”, “a” — these fix the cardinalities. “An employee is assigned to exactly one department” → 1 at the Department end.
  5. Spot the “either/or”. “Companies either are producers or retailers” with different attributes each → that is specialization (an “is a” triangle/diamond), not two separate entities.
  6. Spot the self-link. “An employee can be the boss of one to many other employees” → a relationship from Employee back to itself. Do not invent a “Boss” entity.

Homework 03 Task 1 · Company / Department / Employee

matches the official solution

Write this — the exam answer

Draw it. If you also want words beside the drawing, this is all that is needed:

Entities + keys Company(CompanyID, Name, LegalForm) Department(Dep.ID, Name) Employee(EmployeeID, Name, Birthday) Producer(ProductionCapacity) Retailer(StorageCapacity) Relationships + cardinalities Company 1 --- consists of --- N Department Department 1 --- works for --- N Employee (employee in exactly one dept) Employee 1 --- is head of --- 1 Department Employee 1 --- is boss of --- N Employee (self-link) Company --- is a --- Producer / Retailer (specialization)
If the marker wants a sentence“Company and Department are 1:N because a department belongs to one company. Employee–Department is N:1 because each employee is assigned to exactly one department. ‘is boss of’ is a recursive 1:N relationship on Employee. Producer and Retailer are subtypes of Company.”

Why — the full explanation

Why Department is its own entity and not an attribute of Employee. A department has its own ID and its own name, and many employees share it. Anything with its own identifier that repeats across rows is an entity. If you made it a text attribute on Employee you would store the same department name hundreds of times — the exact problem normalization exists to prevent.

Why “is head of” is 1:1. The text says a department has “a person who is the head”. One head per department; and a person heads at most one department. Both directions answer “one”, so 1:1. This is a separate relationship from “works for” even though both connect Employee and Department — they mean different facts, so they get their own diamonds. Two entities may be joined by several relationships.

Why “is boss of” loops back to Employee. A boss is an employee. Drawing a second box called “Boss” would duplicate the same people. Instead the line leaves Employee and returns to Employee. Cardinality: one employee can boss many (N), and each employee has one boss (1). When you translate this to tables later, it becomes a boss_id column inside Employee pointing at Employee.

Why specialization rather than three entities. Producers and retailers are companies — they share CompanyID, Name, LegalForm — and only add one attribute each. Specialization says “same thing, extra detail”. Two independent entities would force you to duplicate the shared attributes. In the exam, draw the supertype on top, an “is a” connector, and the two subtypes below with only their extra attributes.

Task 2 — what changes when dates arrive. “An employee belongs to a department from some start date to an end date” means the fact now has its own properties. A fact’s properties hang off the diamond, not off either entity: StartDate and EndDate become attributes of the relationship. Do this for all three relationships the task lists. And note the consequence: once a relationship carries dates, the same employee can appear in it more than once, so it stops being a plain 1:N link and behaves like M:N over time.

The four mistakes that cost marks here
  • Forgetting to underline the key attribute — it is the cheapest mark on the page.
  • Writing cardinality on the wrong end. Ask the question out loud, twice.
  • Turning a repeated value (department name, room type) into a text attribute instead of its own entity.
  • Leaving a relationship unnamed. A blank diamond is not an answer; use the verb from the text.

DRILL 2Turn the ER model into tables, then into CREATE TABLE

🔴 Exam-core Prof. Scholz explicitly named the Relational Model as a focus on 22 July 2026; Wrap-Up Tasks 2–4, Learning Labs 05 and 08, and Homework 07 drill it.

Foundation — three rules cover every diagram

Turning a picture into tables is mechanical. There are only three cases, decided by the cardinality you already wrote:

  • 1:N → no new table. Put the key of the “1” side as a column inside the “N” side table. That column is the foreign key. One hotel has many rooms → Room gets a HotelID column.
  • M:N → you must create a new table. It holds the two keys together as its primary key, plus any attributes that were on the diamond. Guests book rooms, many-to-many → new table Books(RoomID, GuestID, StartDate, EndDate).
  • 1:1 → put the foreign key on either side (choose the side that is never empty).

Vocabulary you need: a primary key is the column(s) that identify a row uniquely — never repeated, never empty. A foreign key is a column holding a primary key value from another table; it is how tables are linked, and the database refuses values that do not exist over there.

Wrap-Up Tasks 2–3 · Hotel model → relations → DDL

matches the official solution

Write this — the exam answer

-- step 1: relations, keys underlined Hotel(HotelID, Name, Street, HouseNumber, ZipCode, City) Type(TypeID, Name, Description, Price) Room(RoomID, HotelID→Hotel, TypeID→Type, LivingArea) Guest(GuestID, Name, Street, HouseNumber, ZipCode, City) Books(RoomID→Room, GuestID→Guest, StartDate, EndDate) -- step 2: the two 1:N links folded in, M:N kept as its own table

Then the DDL, one table per relation, parents before children:

CREATE TABLE hm_hotel (
    ho_id      serial PRIMARY KEY,
    ho_name    character varying(50),
    ho_street  character varying(50),
    ho_house_number character varying(5),
    ho_zip_code     character varying(5),
    ho_city    character varying(50)
);
CREATE TABLE hm_room (
    ro_id   serial PRIMARY KEY,
    ro_hotel integer NOT NULL,
    ro_type  integer NOT NULL,
    ro_living_area numeric(4,2),
    CONSTRAINT fk_room_hotel FOREIGN KEY (ro_hotel) REFERENCES hm_hotel (ho_id),
    CONSTRAINT fk_room_type  FOREIGN KEY (ro_type)  REFERENCES hm_type (ty_id)
);
CREATE TABLE hm_books (
    bo_room  integer,
    bo_guest integer,
    bo_start_date date,
    bo_end_date   date,
    PRIMARY KEY (bo_room, bo_guest),
    CONSTRAINT fk_books_room  FOREIGN KEY (bo_room)  REFERENCES hm_room (ro_id),
    CONSTRAINT fk_books_guest FOREIGN KEY (bo_guest) REFERENCES hm_guest (gu_id)
);

Why — the full explanation

Why Room swallowed two foreign keys. Both “includes” (Hotel–Room) and “is of” (Room–Type) are 1:N with Room on the N side. Rule 1 fires twice: the key of the 1 side goes into the N side. So Room gains HotelID and TypeID, and the two relationships vanish as separate tables. This is what “refine the relational model” means in Task 2 — the first draft lists Includes and IsOf as tables, and refining folds them away.

Why Books survived as a table. A guest books many rooms and a room is booked by many guests — M:N. There is no single column you could add to either side without repeating rows. So it becomes its own table whose primary key is the pair, and the dates from the diamond live there.

Why serial and why NOT NULL. serial makes PostgreSQL generate the next integer automatically, which is why the task says “use integer types for the primary keys”. NOT NULL on ro_hotel encodes a modelling fact: a room cannot exist without a hotel. If the model allowed rooms with no hotel, you would leave it nullable. The constraint is the drawing, written down.

Why order matters. A foreign key can only point at a table that already exists, so create Hotel and Type before Room, and Room and Guest before Books. If the exam asks only for one table, say which tables it depends on.

One honest caveat about this official answer. Its hm_books primary key is (bo_room, bo_guest), which silently forbids the same guest booking the same room on two different dates — yet the prompt explicitly asks for that. The faithful key is (bo_room, bo_guest, bo_start_date). Write the official pair if you want to match the marking scheme, and add one line noting the repeat-booking case; that reads as understanding, not disagreement.

DRILL 3Functional dependencies, candidate keys, normal forms

🔴 Exam-core Prof. Scholz explicitly named Normalization as a focus on 22 July 2026; Homework 06, Learning Lab 07, Additional Exercise 2, and the Wrap-Up require it.

Foundation — one idea, then four checks

Functional dependency (FD). Written X → Y, read: “if I know X, then Y is fixed.” That is the whole definition. Test it on the data: pick two rows with the same X — if Y ever differs, it is not an FD.

StudentID → Name every row with 101 has Name = Fred ✓ it holds Name → StudentID Fred is 101 and also 106 ✗ not an FD

Candidate key. A set of columns that (a) determines every other column, and (b) cannot be made smaller. Find it by asking: what is the fewest columns I need to pin down one row?

Prime attribute = a column that is part of some candidate key. Non-prime = everything else. You need the word for the 2NF test.

Now the four checks, in order. Each one assumes the previous passed — if 1NF fails, everything below fails automatically.

  • 1NF — every cell holds a single value. A cell containing “Louvre, Eiffel Tower” breaks it.
  • 2NF — no non-prime column depends on only part of the key. Only ever a problem when the key has two or more columns. Single-column key → 2NF is automatic.
  • 3NF — no non-key column determines another non-key column (no “detour”). Country → CountryPopulation inside a City table is the classic failure.
  • BCNF — for every FD X → Y, X must be a superkey. Stricter than 3NF.

Use the same classroom workflow every time: first write the atomic 1NF relation and its key; use its partial dependencies to build 2NF; use the 2NF relations’ transitive dependencies to build 3NF; then test every resulting relation for BCNF. If a stage needs no split, copy the relations forward and write “unchanged”—do not jump silently from the source table to the final design.

How one split works: take the FD that broke the current stage, put its determinant and dependants in a new relation with the determinant as key, and retain the determinant in the remaining relation as a foreign key. Nothing is deleted; the facts get one clear home.

Notation key — how to read and write the exam syntax

These lines are relational-schema shorthand, not SQL. The arrow has two related but different readings depending on where it appears.

Dependencies and keys

  • {City, Attraction} is a set of attributes. Braces group the columns; their order is irrelevant.
  • City → Country is an FD: equal City values must have equal Country values. Read the arrow as “determines.”
  • Country⁺ is the closure of Country: everything obtainable from Country using the FDs.
  • If X⁺ contains every attribute, X is a superkey. If no proper subset of X still works, X is a candidate key.

Relation schemas

  • CITY(City, Country, …) means a relation/table named CITY with the listed attributes/columns.
  • City PK means City is the chosen primary key — one selected candidate key.
  • Country FK→COUNTRY.Country means CITY.Country is a foreign key referencing COUNTRY.Country. Here the arrow means “references.”
  • PK(CITY_ATTRACTION)={City, Attraction} means the pair is one composite primary key; neither attribute is claimed to be a key alone.
Read this relation line CITY(City PK, Country FK→COUNTRY.Country, CityPopulation, Capital) Table CITY · key City · Country references COUNTRY · two ordinary attributes

Paper rule: use either underlining or explicit PK/FK labels, and stay consistent. When the referenced primary key is obvious, Country FK→COUNTRY is an acceptable shorter form.

What to look at in this prompt
  1. Read the prose under the table, not just the table. It tells you “StudentID is unique per student” and “names are not required to be unique”. Those two sentences decide every FD.
  2. Find the repeated rows. StudentID 101 appears three times — so StudentID alone cannot be the key. What makes those three rows different? The Unit. That is your key hint.
  3. For each column ask “what fixes this value?” Name is fixed by StudentID. Grade needs StudentID and Unit.
  4. Check cells for lists — here every cell has one value, so 1NF passes. (In Task 2 the Attractions column does not.)

Learning Lab 07 Task 1 · Student relation

matches the official solution

Write this — the exam answer

1.1 FDs {StudentID} → {Name, Gender} {StudentID, Unit} → {Grade} 1.2 Candidate key {StudentID, Unit} 1.3 Normalization Original relation verdict: 1NF YES — every cell contains one value 2NF NO — StudentID → Name, Gender is a partial dependency on key {StudentID, Unit} 3NF NO — not in 2NF BCNF NO — not in 3NF Normalize as far as possible: 1NF: STUDENT_1NF(StudentID, Unit, Name, Gender, Grade) PK = {StudentID, Unit} 2NF — split StudentID → Name, Gender: STUDENT(StudentID PK, Name, Gender) STUDENT_UNIT(StudentID FK→STUDENT, Unit, Grade) PK(STUDENT_UNIT) = {StudentID, Unit} 3NF: unchanged — no transitive dependency BCNF: unchanged — every determinant is a key Final BCNF design: STUDENT and STUDENT_UNIT.

Classroom working example · build every stage

The original answer above is already correct. The sequence below expands its decomposition into the 1NF → 2NF → 3NF → BCNF working used in class.

1NF ✓
Write the atomic starting relation
STUDENT_1NF(StudentID, Unit, Name, Gender, Grade)

Every cell is atomic. Candidate key: (StudentID, Unit).

StudentID → Name, Gender is partial — split it out ↓
2NF ✓
Build 2NF from the 1NF relation
STUDENT(StudentID, Name, Gender)STUDENT_UNIT(StudentID, Unit, Grade) · StudentID FK → STUDENT

Name and Gender now depend on the whole key of STUDENT; Grade depends on the whole composite key of STUDENT_UNIT.

No transitive dependency in either 2NF relation ↓
3NF ✓
No new split: carry the two 2NF relations forward

STUDENT and STUDENT_UNIT are already in 3NF.

Test every non-trivial FD’s left side ↓
BCNF ✓
No new split: the 3NF design is already BCNF

StudentID is a key of STUDENT; (StudentID, Unit) is a key of STUDENT_UNIT. Every determinant is therefore a superkey of its own relation.

Final BCNF design: STUDENT(StudentID, Name, Gender) and STUDENT_UNIT(StudentID, Unit, Grade).

The sentence that earns the 2NF split“In STUDENT_1NF, Name and Gender depend on StudentID, a proper subset of candidate key (StudentID, Unit); therefore split off STUDENT(StudentID, Name, Gender).”

Why — the full explanation

Why the key is the pair. One row is one grade. To point at exactly one grade you must say which student and which unit — student 101 has three grades, and “Mathematics” is taken by several students. Neither column alone is enough, and together they are enough, so {StudentID, Unit} is minimal and therefore a candidate key.

Why Name → StudentID is not an FD. Tempting, because names look identifying. But the prose warns you: Fred is 101 and Fred is also 106. Two rows share a Name and disagree on StudentID, so the dependency fails. This is exactly why the prose is printed — it is not decoration.

What “partial dependency” actually means. The key has two parts. Gender is decided by only one of them. So if student 102 takes four units, her Name and Gender are copied into four rows. That duplication is the disease; 2NF is the rule that names it. Split so each fact is stored once: identity facts in Student, performance facts in StudentUnit.

Separate the source verdict from the repaired design. The original 1NF relation is not in 2NF, so that original relation is also not in 3NF or BCNF. After the 2NF split, however, the new relations pass 3NF and BCNF. Write both facts; “not 3NF” describes the starting table, while “final design is BCNF” describes the result.

Check your decomposition is lossless. The two new tables share StudentID. Joining them back on StudentID reproduces the original rows exactly, with nothing invented and nothing lost. That shared column is the test: if the pieces had no column in common, the split would be wrong.

Paper layout Draw four labelled rows: 1NF, 2NF, 3NF, BCNF. Put the relation schemas in each row; beside every arrow write the FD that causes the next split. If there is no split, write “unchanged” and one pass reason.

NF working: write 1NF schema+key → split partial FDs for 2NF → split transitive FDs for 3NF → in each relation, every determinant must be a key for BCNF.

Learning Lab 07 Task 2 · City / country table

matches the official solution

Write this — the exam answer

2.1 Functional dependencies Before 1NF: {City} → {Country, CityPopulation, CountryPopulation, Capital, Attractions-list} {Country} → {CountryPopulation} After 1NF: {City} → {Country, CityPopulation, CountryPopulation, Capital} {Country} → {CountryPopulation} City does not determine Attraction. 2.2 Candidate keys Before 1NF: {City} After 1NF: {City, Attraction} {Country} is not a candidate key: Country⁺ = {Country, CountryPopulation}. 2.3 Normalization Original relation verdict: 1NF NO — Attractions holds several values in one cell 2NF NO — not in 1NF 3NF NO — not in 2NF; also City → Country → CountryPopulation BCNF NO — not in 3NF Normalize as far as possible: 1NF — one row per attraction: CITY_FACT_1NF(City, Attraction, Country, CityPopulation, CountryPopulation, Capital) PK = {City, Attraction} 2NF — split the partial dependency on City: CITY_2NF(City PK, Country, CityPopulation, CountryPopulation, Capital) CITY_ATTRACTION(City FK→CITY_2NF, Attraction) PK(CITY_ATTRACTION) = {City, Attraction} 3NF — split Country → CountryPopulation: COUNTRY(Country PK, CountryPopulation) CITY(City PK, Country FK→COUNTRY, CityPopulation, Capital) CITY_ATTRACTION(City FK→CITY, Attraction) PK(CITY_ATTRACTION) = {City, Attraction} BCNF: unchanged — every determinant is a key Final BCNF design: COUNTRY, CITY, CITY_ATTRACTION.

Classroom working example · build every stage

The original answer above is the concise solution. The sequence below shows how to arrive at those final relations one normal form at a time.

SOURCE ✗
The displayed table is not in 1NF

Attractions contains lists such as “Louvre, Eiffel Tower”. Build one row per attraction.

Explode the repeating Attractions group ↓
1NF ✓
Atomic wide relation
CITY_FACT_1NF(City, Attraction, Country, CityPopulation, CountryPopulation, Capital)

Candidate key after the explosion: (City, Attraction).

City determines all city facts — a proper-subset dependency ↓
2NF ✓
Split facts that depend on City alone
CITY_2NF(City, Country, CityPopulation, CountryPopulation, Capital)CITY_ATTRACTION(City, Attraction) · City FK → CITY_2NF

Every non-prime attribute now depends on the whole key of its relation.

Country → CountryPopulation is transitive inside CITY_2NF ↓
3NF ✓
Give the country fact its own relation
COUNTRY(Country, CountryPopulation)CITY(City, Country, CityPopulation, Capital) · Country FK → COUNTRYCITY_ATTRACTION(City, Attraction) · City FK → CITY
Test each remaining determinant ↓
BCNF ✓
No new split: the 3NF design is already BCNF

Country, City, and (City, Attraction) are keys of their respective relations, so every non-trivial determinant is a superkey.

Final BCNF design: COUNTRY, CITY, and CITY_ATTRACTION as shown above.

Why — the full explanation

The 1NF break is the visible one. “Louvre, Eiffel Tower” is two facts in one cell. You cannot search, count, or delete one attraction without string surgery. The fix is a row per attraction, which is why Attractions becomes its own table and the key of that table is the pair {City, Attraction}.

The 3NF break is the one people miss. CountryPopulation is a fact about the country, not about the city. The chain is City → Country → CountryPopulation: a non-key column determined by another non-key column. Consequence: France’s population is written three times (Paris, Lyon, Marseille), and correcting it means finding every row. Pull it into a Country table and store it once.

Why the key changes after the 1NF fix. Before the fix, one row per city, so {City} identifies it. After splitting attractions into their own rows, a city appears several times in that table, so you need City plus Attraction to pin one row. This is worth a sentence in the exam — the official answer states both keys.

Why Capital stays in City. Capital is yes/no for that city. It genuinely depends on City, not on Country, so it belongs in the City table. (You could argue Country → capital-city, but the column as written describes the city.)

Paper layout Start with the non-1NF source, then write the five-column 1NF wide relation with key (City, Attraction). Do not jump straight to three final tables: show the City-only 2NF split first, then remove CountryPopulation for 3NF, then state why no BCNF split remains.

Repeating group → one 1NF row per value and recompute key; then City-only facts → CITY, CountryPopulation → COUNTRY, pair fact → CITY_ATTRACTION.

Foundation — finding candidate keys mechanically (the closure method)

With no story to reason about, use the algorithm. The closure of a set X, written X⁺, is everything you can reach by repeatedly applying the FDs.

Given: A→B, CD→A, BC→D, AE→F, CE→F over ABCDEF 1. Which letters never appear on the RIGHT of any arrow? C and E → they can never be derived, so EVERY key must contain C and E. 2. Start from {C,E} and close it: CE⁺ = C,E, +F (CE→F) = {C,E,F} ← missing A,B,D, so CE is not a key. 3. Add one more letter at a time and close: ACE⁺ : A,C,E +B (A→B) +F (AE→F) +D (BC→D) = ALL ✓ key BCE⁺ : B,C,E +D (BC→D) +A (CD→A) +F = ALL ✓ key CDE⁺ : C,D,E +A (CD→A) +B (A→B) +F = ALL ✓ key

Stop as soon as a set reaches all six letters, and never test a superset of something that already worked (keys must be minimal).

Learning Lab 07 Task 3 · Abstract relation ABCDEF

official verdict + verified extension

Write this — the exam answer

3.1 Candidate keys ACE, BCE, CDE (C and E are in every key: neither ever appears on the right of an arrow) 3.2 Original answer No. Not even in 2NF: F depends on AE and on CE, each only part of a candidate key — a partial dependency. Not in BCNF: for example, A→B while A is not a superkey. Supplied decomposition AB BCD AEF

Worked BCNF example · optional extension

Task 3.2 asks only for the BCNF verdict. The cards below keep that original answer intact and show one independently checked lossless BCNF attempt as extra practice.

BCNF ✗
The asked-for verdict
R(A,B,C,D,E,F)

A → B is one sufficient counterexample: A+ = AB, not all attributes.

Optional generated extension: decompose on CE → F, then A → B, then CD → A ↓
BCNF ✓
One lossless BCNF result
CEF(C,E, F)AB(A, B)ACD(A,C, D) · alternate key (C,D)CDE(C,D,E)

Every decomposition step is lossless. This extension is not required by Task 3.2.

Exam stopping point: “Not in BCNF because A → B and A is not a superkey.”

Why — the full explanation

Why start with “what never appears on the right”. If a letter is never produced by any FD, no combination of other letters can ever give it to you — so it must be handed to you in the key itself. C and E qualify, which instantly shrinks the search from 63 possible subsets to a handful. This trick alone usually finds the keys in under a minute.

Why three keys and not one. Once you have C and E, you need something that eventually yields A, B and D. Adding A works (A→B, then BC→D). Adding B works (BC→D, then CD→A). Adding D works (CD→A, then A→B). Three different minimal ways in, so three candidate keys — all equally valid.

Why it fails 2NF, not merely BCNF. Take AE→F. The candidate key containing A and E is ACE. AE is a proper part of it, and F is non-prime (F is in no key). A non-prime attribute depending on part of a key is precisely the 2NF violation. Naming the specific FD and the specific key is what earns the mark — “it is not in BCNF” alone does not.

Why the optional BCNF result is labelled carefully. The source asks only for the verdict. The generated decomposition CEF, AB, ACD, CDE is lossless and every result is in BCNF, but it does not preserve BC→D and AE→F as constraints that can be checked inside one table. BCNF can sacrifice dependency preservation; say so if you volunteer the decomposition.

Paper rule For the asked task, stop after one violating FD and a closure showing its determinant is not a superkey. Only decompose if the question asks; at each BCNF split write the violating FD and test the two resulting schemas again.

BCNF failure proof: name X→Y, show X⁺ ≠ all attributes. A lossless BCNF split can lose dependency preservation—check both properties separately.

Normalization in four lines, for the exam1NF one value per cell · 2NF nothing depends on part of the key · 3NF no non-key → non-key detour · BCNF every arrow starts at a superkey. Always answer all four in order, and say which FD breaks the rule.

DRILL 4Relational algebra

🔴 Exam-core Prof. Scholz explicitly named Relational Algebra as a focus on 22 July 2026; it is drilled in Homework 05 and Learning Lab 06.

Foundation — five symbols, and they map onto SQL you already read

Relational algebra is SQL with mathematical notation. Each operator takes tables in and gives a table out, so you can nest them.

SymbolNamePlain meaningSQL equivalent
σ sigmaselectionkeep the rows that match a conditionWHERE
π piprojectionkeep the columns you list (drops duplicates)SELECT DISTINCT
⋈joinglue two tables where a condition matchesJOIN … ON
−differencein the first, not in the secondNOT IN / EXCEPT
∩ ∪intersect / unionin both / in eitherINTERSECT / UNION

The one habit that makes these easy: read the expression from the inside out, and build it in this order —

1. σ first cut rows down as early as possible 2. ⋈ next join only what survived, matching key = key 3. set ops ∩ ∪ − if the sentence says "and also" / "or" / "not" 4. π last finally keep only the asked-for columns πName( σStudy='Economics'( Student ) ) └ step 4 ┘ └──── step 1 ────┘

Subscripts. The condition rides under the symbol: σPlaces=2(Room). The join condition rides under the bowtie: A ⋈A.x=B.x B. When two tables both have a “Name” column, write the table in front: Student.Name.

What to look at in an algebra prompt
  1. Which columns does it ask to show? That is your outermost π. “Find the names” → πName.
  2. Which conditions are stated? Each becomes a σ. “that study economics” → σStudy='Economics'.
  3. Do the columns you need live in more than one table? If yes you need a join, and the join column is the shared key (Student# with Student#, Lecture# with Lecture#).
  4. Listen for the set-op words. “and the course …” meaning both → ∩. “do not” → −.
  5. Passed vs failed. German grades: 1.0 best, 4.0 still a pass, 5.0 fail. “passed” → Grade ≤ 4.0; “failed” → Grade > 4.0.

Learning Lab 06 · The six queries

matches the official solution

Write this — the exam answer

1.1 names of students studying economics πName( σStudy='Economics'(Student) ) 1.2 professors in a room with two places πProfessor.Name( Professor ⋈Professor.Room#=Room.Room# σPlaces=2(Room) ) 1.3 courses taking place on Wednesday πLecture.Title( Lecture ⋈Lecture.Lecture#=TakesPlace.Lecture# σWeekday='Wednesday'(TakesPlace) ) 1.4 students who passed BOTH 'Operations Research' AND 'Information Systems' πStudent.Name( Student ⋈ σGrade<=4.0(Examines) ⋈ σTitle='Operations Research'(Lecture) ) ∩ πStudent.Name( Student ⋈ σGrade<=4.0(Examines) ⋈ σTitle='Information Systems'(Lecture) ) 1.5 students that do not attend any course πStudent.Name( Student ⋈ ( πStudent#(Student) − πStudent#(Attends) ) ) 1.6 students who failed in WT2023, with the course name πStudent.Name, Lecture.Title( Lecture ⋈ Student ⋈ σSemester='WT2023' ∧ Grade>4.0(Examines) )
Operations tree question (Task 2)Read a tree bottom-up. σName=Konstantin Pfeiffer on Professor → πProfessor# gives 004 → join into TakesPlace → πWeekday,Timeslot. Answer: (Thursday, 10-12) and (Wednesday, 14-16) — the two slots professor 004 teaches.

Why — the full explanation

1.1 needs no join because Study and Name are both inside Student. Whenever every column mentioned lives in one table, the answer is just π(σ(table)) — do not add joins for decoration.

1.2 and 1.3 are the standard shape. The filter applies to one table, then you join to reach the column you must display. Note the σ sits inside the join: filter Room down to the 2-place rooms first, then join. Filtering before joining is both cheaper and easier to write.

Why 1.4 needs ∩ and not a single σ with “and”. The condition is about two different rows of Examines — one exam for Operations Research, another for Information Systems. A single row can never satisfy Title='OR' ∧ Title='IS'; that would return nothing. So compute the set of students who passed the first course, compute the set who passed the second, and intersect. This is the standard trick whenever a prompt says “both X and Y” about repeated facts.

Why 1.5 uses difference and then joins back. “Students that do not attend courses” is an absence, and algebra expresses absence with −. Take all Student# and subtract the Student# that appear in Attends; what remains are the non-attenders — but only their IDs. The prompt asks for names, so join that set back to Student to pick up the Name column. Forgetting the join back is the most common error here.

Why 1.6 puts both conditions in one σ. Semester and Grade describe the same exam row, so a single selection with ∧ works. Then two joins bring in the student’s name and the lecture’s title, and the final π shows both columns as asked.

Reading trees in general. Leaves are tables; you evaluate upward; each node consumes what is below it. If asked for “the resulting relation”, give the actual rows, not a description — check them against the printed data.

DRILL 5Write the SQL query

🔴 Exam-core Prof. Scholz explicitly named SQL as a focus on 22 July 2026; Homework 08, Learning Lab 09, Wrap-Up 5, and Additional 4 are query sets.

Foundation — write the clauses in this order, every time

A SELECT has at most six clauses and they must appear in this order. You can memorise the skeleton and fill the blanks:

SELECT which columns to show (and aggregates: COUNT, SUM, AVG) FROM the first table JOIN … ON key = key (repeat for each extra table) WHERE filter individual ROWS (no aggregates allowed here) GROUP BY one row per what? HAVING filter the GROUPS (aggregates allowed here) ORDER BY … ASC | DESC

The single most useful idea: “what is one row of my answer?” Decide that first, and everything follows.

  • One row per hotel with a count → GROUP BY hotel.
  • One row per room → no GROUP BY at all.
  • A single number → an aggregate with no GROUP BY.

WHERE vs HAVING — the distinction the exam loves. WHERE runs before grouping and cannot see SUM/COUNT. HAVING runs after grouping and exists precisely to filter on them. “customers who spent more than 5000 in total” is a HAVING; “orders after 2024-01-01” is a WHERE.

Joining: put the tables in a chain along the foreign keys. To get from Guest to Hotel in the hotel database you must pass through Books and Room — you cannot jump, because no column links them directly.

Small tools: DISTINCT removes duplicate rows (“listed only once”). LIKE 'A%' = starts with A; LIKE '%burg' = ends with burg. COUNT(*) counts rows; SUM(a*b) multiplies then totals.

What to look at in a query prompt
  1. “Select the …” tells you the SELECT list. “the name and the number of visits” → two output columns, one of them a COUNT.
  2. “per / for each” means GROUP BY. “number of bookings per hotel” → group by hotel.
  3. “only once” means DISTINCT.
  4. “more than / below” after a total means HAVING. Before a total it means WHERE.
  5. “sorted / order by … descending” means ORDER BY … DESC. Easy mark; do not drop it.
  6. List the tables you must touch and chain them by foreign key before writing a single word of SQL.

Wrap-Up Task 5 · Six hotel queries

matches the official solution

Write this — the exam answer

5.1.1 ID of rooms cheaper than 300 SELECT ro_id FROM hm_room JOIN hm_type ON ro_type = ty_id WHERE ty_price < 300; 5.1.2 ID + type, living area 20–50, ID descending SELECT ro_id, ty_name FROM hm_room JOIN hm_type ON ro_type = ty_id WHERE ro_living_area > 20 AND ro_living_area < 50 ORDER BY ro_id DESC; 5.2.1 hotels offering a King Size Apartment, once each SELECT DISTINCT ho_name FROM hm_hotel JOIN hm_room ON ho_id = ro_hotel JOIN hm_type ON ro_type = ty_id WHERE ty_name = 'King Size Apartment'; 5.2.2 hotel name + number of bookings per hotel SELECT ho_name, COUNT(*) AS visits FROM hm_hotel JOIN hm_room ON ho_id = ro_hotel JOIN hm_books ON bo_room = ro_id GROUP BY ho_id; 5.3.1 guests who ever booked in the Grand Hotel, once each SELECT DISTINCT gu_name FROM hm_guest JOIN hm_books ON gu_id = bo_guest JOIN hm_room ON ro_id = bo_room JOIN hm_hotel ON ho_id = ro_hotel WHERE ho_name = 'Grand Hotel'; 5.3.2 guests who spent more than 800 in total, with the amount SELECT gu_name, SUM((bo_end_date - bo_start_date) * ty_price) AS spent FROM hm_guest JOIN hm_books ON gu_id = bo_guest JOIN hm_room ON ro_id = bo_room JOIN hm_type ON ro_type = ty_id GROUP BY gu_id HAVING SUM((bo_end_date - bo_start_date) * ty_price) > 800;

Why — the full explanation

Why the price query needs a join at all. Price does not live in Room — it lives in Type, because every Single Apartment costs the same. So to filter rooms by price you must reach across the ro_type → ty_id foreign key. Whenever a condition names something the table does not contain, that is your signal to join.

Why 5.2.1 needs DISTINCT. The Grand Hotel has several King Size rooms, so the join produces one row per room and the hotel name repeats. The prompt says “listed only once”, so collapse them. Note the rule: DISTINCT is about the output rows, not the joins.

Why 5.2.2 groups by ho_id and not ho_name. Two hotels could share a name; the ID cannot. Grouping by the key is always safe. (PostgreSQL permits selecting ho_name here because it is functionally dependent on the grouped primary key.) COUNT(*) counts the rows in each group, and after the two joins each row is exactly one booking — which is what “number of visits” means.

Why 5.3.1 chains four tables. Guest and Hotel share no column. The path is Guest → Books (who booked) → Room (which room) → Hotel (whose hotel). Write the chain down before typing; every JOIN is one link, and each ON is the foreign key equals the primary key it references.

The arithmetic in 5.3.2. Subtracting two date values in PostgreSQL yields an integer number of nights. Times the nightly price gives the cost of one booking; SUM over the guest’s group gives the total. The condition is on that total, so it must be HAVING, and the aggregate is repeated there because an alias defined in SELECT is not visible to HAVING.

Two extra shapes from the Additional Exercise set. (a) “customers who never bought a product starting with A” → a negative, so use WHERE cs_customer_id NOT IN (SELECT … LIKE 'A%'). (b) “revenue for men and women separately” → GROUP BY cs_gender. Both are the same skeleton with a different blank filled in.

Marks people throw away on SQL
  • Forgetting ORDER BY … DESC when the prompt says “descending”.
  • Putting an aggregate in WHERE. It must be HAVING.
  • Missing DISTINCT after “only once in the result set”.
  • Joining two tables that share no key — trace the chain instead.
  • Ending without a semicolon, or renaming a computed column without AS when the prompt asks to “show the amount”.

DRILL 6Knowledge questions — definitions you may be asked to state

🔴 Exam-core The final-exam slide lists “knowledge questions” as its own area; the architecture homework and lab are entirely of this type.

Foundation — the shape of a full-mark definition

A one-word answer rarely scores. Use the same four-beat structure every time, and keep it to three or four lines:

1. What it is one sentence, category first 2. How it works the mechanism in one sentence 3. Why it matters the problem it solves 4. Example one concrete instance from the course

Answer bank · the definitions most likely to be asked

written to the four-beat shape

Write this — model answers

Primary key Column(s) that identify each row uniquely. Never NULL, never repeated. Enforced by the DBMS. Example: ho_id in hm_hotel. Foreign key Column holding a primary-key value of another table; it links the two. The DBMS rejects values that do not exist there (referential integrity). Example: ro_hotel → hm_hotel(ho_id). Functional dependency X → Y If two rows agree on X they must agree on Y — knowing X fixes Y. Used to find keys and to decide normal forms. Example: StudentID → Name. Normalization Splitting tables so each fact is stored once, guided by FDs. Removes update/insert/delete anomalies and redundancy. Cost: more joins when querying. 3NF In 2NF and no non-key attribute depends on another non-key attribute. Example violation: City → Country → CountryPopulation. Transaction / ACID A unit of work that must happen completely or not at all. Atomicity all-or-nothing · Consistency rules still hold · Isolation concurrent transactions do not corrupt each other · Durability committed data survives a crash. Three-level architecture (ANSI/SPARC) External = per-user views · Conceptual = the logical schema · Internal = physical storage. Separating them gives data independence: storage can change without breaking programs. DDL vs DML DDL defines structure: CREATE, ALTER, DROP. DML changes/reads data: INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, SELECT. View A stored query used like a table. Simplifies access and can hide columns. Not stored data — computed on use. Index Extra structure making lookups fast. Speeds reads, slows writes, uses space. Trigger Procedure the DBMS runs automatically on INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE. Used for auditing or enforcing rules code cannot bypass.

Why — how to handle a definition you did not revise

Fall back on the four beats. Even without the textbook phrasing, “it is a kind of X, it works by Y, it solves Z, for example W” reads as understanding. Markers reward the mechanism and the consequence more than the exact wording.

Prefer a course example over a generic one. Naming hm_room.ro_hotel shows you can apply the idea to the material you were taught; naming “a table in some database” does not.

If asked to compare, give the trade-off. Normalization vs redundancy, index read-speed vs write-cost, view convenience vs recomputation. A comparison question wants both directions, not a list of virtues.

Watch the language. The exam is English and you may bring a dictionary — use it for the prompt wording rather than guessing what a term means. A misread verb (“list” vs “count”) changes the whole answer.

Now do thisCover the “Write this” blocks and redo each drill on paper — Drill 1 (ER), Drill 3 Task 1 (normalization), Drill 4 queries 1.4 and 1.5, and Drill 5 queries 5.2.2 and 5.3.2. Those five are the ones that transfer to the largest share of exam marks. Then use chapters 1–6 below for anything that still felt shaky.
1

ER modelling: turn prose into constraints

Draw what the requirements permit and forbid—not merely a picture of nouns.

🔴 Exam-core Prof. Scholz explicitly named ERM as a focus on 22 July 2026; the final-exam slide, Homework 03, Learning Labs 03–05, and Wrap-Up Task 1 corroborate it.

An ER answer earns its value from four decisions: entity boundaries, identifiers, relationship meaning, and cardinalities. Attributes are the easy part.

Entity

A thing with its own identity and several occurrences: Hotel, Room, Guest. Underline or otherwise mark the key attribute.

Relationship

A fact connecting occurrences: Hotel includes Room; Guest books Room. Dates belong to BOOKS because they describe that fact.

Cardinality

Ask in both directions: “one hotel includes how many rooms?” and “one room belongs to how many hotels?” Write both ends.

Recognition rules

WordingModel moveCheck
“each X has exactly one Y”X participates in an N:1 relationship to Y; X side is mandatory.Can an X exist with zero Y? No.
“zero or many”Optional many participation.Include 0 in the minimum if min/max notation is used.
“for each order/booking…”Attribute of the relationship, or an associative entity when the occurrence needs identity.Would the value change for a different pairing/event?
“types will grow”VehicleType is data in an entity, not five hard-coded subtypes.Adding a type requires INSERT, not schema change.
“either producer or retailer”Specialization. Mark disjointness; mark total only when every supertype occurrence must be one subtype.Can one company be both? Can it be neither?

Wrap-Up 1 · Hotel ER model

independently checked answer

Exam answer

Given nouns & verbs
ER conventions
Cardinality decisions
Final model

HOTEL 1:N ROOM; ROOM N:1 TYPE; GUEST M:N ROOM through BOOKS(start_date, end_date). HOTEL and GUEST each have a composite address. Keys: hotel_id, room_id, type_id, guest_id.

Why each move is there

  • Room belongs to one hotel: the wording “hotels consist of rooms” and globally stated room ID support HOTEL 1:N ROOM.
  • Type is an entity: description and price depend on a reusable type, not on an individual room.
  • BOOKS is M:N: a guest may book several rooms over time and a room is booked by several guests over time.
  • Dates are relationship attributes: they vary per guest–room booking. They later participate in the booking key.
Fast hand-draw recipe
Rectangles and underlined IDs first → three verb diamonds → cardinalities in both directions → relationship dates → remaining attributes. Write the relational key warning room_id + guest_id + start_date in the margin.

M:N event → bridge(FK₁, FK₂, event discriminator, event attributes); include the discriminator in the key when repeats are allowed.

Two high-yield variants

History turns a simple link into an event

Homework 03 adds start/end dates to WORKS_FOR, HEADS, and BOSSES. Each becomes a history relation in the relational model. A useful key is normally the participants plus start_date; add CHECK (end_date IS NULL OR end_date > start_date).

Extensible type lists are data

Learning Lab 03 says CARESE will offer more vehicle types without changing the ER model. Therefore VEHICLE_TYPE is an entity; VEHICLE–TYPE is M:N, and RESERVATION links Customer, VehicleType, and Location with pickup/return dates.

Drill · Insurance model (Learning Lab 03.1)

generated solution

Exam answer

CUSTOMER 1:N CAR; CAR 1:N ACCIDENT (0 allowed on Accident side); POLICY M:N CAR; POLICY 1:N PREMIUM_PAYMENT. PAYMENT has period_start, period_end, due_date, received_date. Use IDs for all entities and VIN as a candidate key for CAR.

Breakdown

“Associated with” does not make Accident an attribute: accidents repeat and have their own facts. A payment is not a multivalued amount; it has dates and therefore deserves an entity. The prompt says customers own one or more cars, so Customer participation in OWNS is total.

Paper check Can one policy cover multiple cars? yes. Can one car be on several historical policies? the wording permits it, so M:N is safest unless a time rule says otherwise.

A repeating fact with its own dates/amounts is an entity or relationship occurrence, never a comma-separated attribute.

2

From ER model to relations and PostgreSQL

The model is not finished until every relationship has a home, every table has a key, and the constraints express the prompt.

🔴 Exam-core Prof. Scholz explicitly named the Relational Model as a focus on 22 July 2026; Wrap-Up Tasks 2–4 and Learning Labs 05 and 08 use the mapping pipeline.

The mapping rules you must be able to reproduce

ER structureRelational mappingTypical key
Strong entityOne table containing atomic attributes.Entity identifier.
Composite attributeStore its components, not the parent label.Unchanged.
1:N relationshipMove the 1-side key into the N-side table as FK. Put relationship attributes there if each N occurrence has at most one relationship occurrence.N-side PK.
1:1 relationshipPlace FK on the mandatory side; add UNIQUE. Separate table if both optional or the relationship has a life of its own.FK is UNIQUE.
M:N relationshipCreate bridge with both FKs and relationship attributes.Both FKs, plus any event discriminator needed for repeats.
SubtypeSupertype table plus subtype table whose PK is also FK to supertype.Inherited supertype ID.
Recursive 1:NNullable self-FK on the child/subordinate row.Entity PK; self-FK is not the key.

Wrap-Up 2 · Correct relational model

exam-ready relation lines

Exam answer

HOTEL(hotel_id, name, street, house_no, zip_code, city) ROOM_TYPE(type_id, name, description, price) ROOM(room_id, hotel_id FK→HOTEL, type_id FK→ROOM_TYPE, living_area) GUEST(guest_id, name, street, house_no, zip_code, city) BOOKING(room_id FK→ROOM, guest_id FK→GUEST, start_date, end_date)

Primary key of BOOKING = (room_id, guest_id, start_date).

Breakdown

INCLUDES and IS_OF are 1:N, so their foreign keys move into ROOM. BOOKS remains a table because it is M:N and has dates. ZIP codes and house numbers are character data: leading zeroes and letters such as “15b” are meaningful.

Verified correction to the supplied solutionThe supplied primary key (bo_room, bo_guest) contradicts the prompt’s explicit requirement that one guest may book the same room at different dates. Adding bo_start_date distinguishes those occurrences. The refined supplied model also labels ZIP as integer although its own SQL correctly uses character data.
Paper recipe Write all entity relations → cross out 1:N relationship tables after moving their FK/attributes → keep M:N bridges → underline the smallest determinant that uniquely names each row → annotate every FK target.

1:N → FK on N; M:N → bridge; 1:1 → FK on mandatory side + UNIQUE; subtype PK is also FK.

Wrap-Up 3–4 · Complete DDL and population

PostgreSQL · corrected and complete

Exam answer

CREATE TABLE hm_hotel (
  ho_id integer PRIMARY KEY,
  ho_name varchar(50) NOT NULL,
  ho_street varchar(50) NOT NULL,
  ho_house_number varchar(8) NOT NULL,
  ho_zip_code varchar(10) NOT NULL,
  ho_city varchar(50) NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE hm_type (
  ty_id integer PRIMARY KEY,
  ty_name varchar(50) NOT NULL UNIQUE,
  ty_description text,
  ty_price numeric(7,2) NOT NULL CHECK (ty_price >= 0)
);

CREATE TABLE hm_room (
  ro_id integer PRIMARY KEY,
  ro_hotel integer NOT NULL REFERENCES hm_hotel(ho_id),
  ro_type integer NOT NULL REFERENCES hm_type(ty_id),
  ro_living_area numeric(6,2) NOT NULL CHECK (ro_living_area > 0)
);

CREATE TABLE hm_guest (
  gu_id integer PRIMARY KEY,
  gu_name varchar(80) NOT NULL,
  gu_street varchar(80) NOT NULL,
  gu_house_number varchar(8) NOT NULL,
  gu_zip_code varchar(10) NOT NULL,
  gu_city varchar(50) NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE hm_booking (
  bo_room integer REFERENCES hm_room(ro_id),
  bo_guest integer REFERENCES hm_guest(gu_id),
  bo_start_date date NOT NULL,
  bo_end_date date NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (bo_room, bo_guest, bo_start_date),
  CHECK (bo_end_date > bo_start_date)
);

Where the marks live

  • Structure: create referenced tables before tables that contain FKs.
  • Integrity: mandatory facts are NOT NULL; prices/areas/date order use CHECK.
  • Domains: use exact numeric for money and text-like types for ZIP/house number.
  • Population: one row per entity or event; the comma-separated source cells disappear.
No-calculator procedure For DDL, draw a five-row dependency order (Hotel, Type, Guest → Room → Booking), then write CREATE statements in that order. On paper, full constraint names are optional unless asked; correct columns and targets are not.

DDL audit: PK every table; FK target exists; mandatory→NOT NULL; domain→CHECK; exact money→numeric; identifiers such as ZIP/card/phone→text.

Constraint patterns worth recognizing

Change a schema

ALTER TABLE aircraft
  RENAME COLUMN range TO max_distance;

ALTER TABLE flight
  ALTER COLUMN status SET DEFAULT 'On Time';

ALTER TABLE airport
  ADD CHECK (airport_code ~ '^[A-Za-z]');

The regular expression tests the first character. The supplied range comparison >= 'aaa' AND <= 'ZZZ' is collation-dependent and reverses lexical case ranges in many collations.

Foreign-key actions

ON DELETE CASCADE removes dependent facts; SET NULL preserves the row but removes the link; RESTRICT/NO ACTION prevents the delete while references remain.

Never choose an action from habit: state the business effect. Message history, for example, may need a soft-deleted user rather than cascading all messages.

3

Normalization: make every fact live once

Use functional dependencies to prove the design; do not normalize by aesthetic instinct.

🔴 Exam-core Prof. Scholz explicitly named Normalization as a focus on 22 July 2026; it recurs in Homework 06–07, Learning Lab 07, the Wrap-Up, and Additional Exercises.

Functional dependencies and closure

A functional dependency X → Y means: whenever two valid rows agree on X, they must agree on Y. It is a statement about all valid states allowed by the semantics—not a coincidence in the sample rows.

Find a candidate key

  1. Put into your start set every attribute that never appears on any non-trivial FD right-hand side.
  2. Compute closure: if an FD’s left side is contained, add its right side.
  3. If closure contains every attribute, you have a superkey.
  4. Remove each start attribute once. If closure stops covering all attributes every time, the key is minimal.

Separate three words

Superkey: uniquely determines all attributes, possibly with extras.
Candidate key: minimal superkey.
Prime attribute: appears in at least one candidate key.

“Minimal” means no proper subset still determines the relation; it does not mean “fewest columns among all keys.”

Homework 06.2 · Candidate key by closure

machine-verified closure

Exam answer

R(A,B,C,D,E), F = { A→C, E→D, B→C }

Attributes absent from every RHS are A, B, E, so every key must contain ABE.

(ABE)+ = ABE → add C using A→C (or B→C) → add D using E→D = ABCDE.

Candidate key = {A,B,E}. R is not BCNF because A, B, and E are not superkeys although each determines a non-trivial attribute.

Minimality and normal forms

Remove A: BE cannot derive A. Remove B: AE cannot derive B. Remove E: AB cannot derive D or E. Therefore the superkey is minimal. It also violates 2NF because C depends on proper subsets A and B, and D depends on E.

No-calculator closure layout Write ABE | +C | +D = ABCDE. Under it, write three one-line removal tests. This is faster and more markable than prose.

Key by closure: start with attributes absent from RHS; expand; then prove minimality by removing each attribute once.

The four normal forms—precise enough for an exam

FormConditionViolation smell
1NFEach cell contains one value from its domain; no repeating group in one cell.aid = "1,5" or attractions = "Louvre, Eiffel Tower".
2NF1NF, and no non-prime attribute depends on a proper subset of any candidate key.With key (sid,aid), student name depends on sid alone.
3NFFor every non-trivial X→A, X is a superkey or A is prime.sid→class and class→leader causes leader to depend transitively on sid.
BCNFFor every non-trivial X→Y, X is a superkey.Any determinant that is not a superkey.
Safe wordingDo not define 3NF merely as “all non-key attributes are independent.” Use the determinant/prime-attribute rule above; it handles relations with multiple candidate keys correctly.

Homework 06.1 · School database to BCNF

complete by-hand solution

Exam answer

After splitting repeating groups, use SCHOOL(sid, name, class, leader, aid, activity, hours).

FDs: sid→name,class; class→leader; aid→activity; (sid,aid)→hours.

(sid,aid)+ = sid,aid,name,class,leader,activity,hours, so (sid,aid) is the candidate key.

STUDENT(sid, name, class FK→CLASS) CLASS(class, leader) ACTIVITY(aid, activity) PARTICIPATION(sid FK→STUDENT, aid FK→ACTIVITY, hours)

Each resulting determinant is a key of its relation, so the decomposition is BCNF under the stated FDs.

Classroom working example · build every stage

The original final relations above remain the answer. This example exposes the intermediate 1NF, 2NF, and 3NF schemas.

1NF ✓
Explode each activity list
SCHOOL_1NF(sid, aid, name, class, leader, activity, hours)
sid → name, class, leader and aid → activity are partial dependencies ↓
2NF ✓
Split student-only and activity-only facts
STUDENT_2NF(sid, name, class, leader)ACTIVITY(aid, activity)PARTICIPATION(sid, aid, hours)
sid → class → leader is transitive inside STUDENT_2NF ↓
3NF ✓
Split the class fact
STUDENT(sid, name, class FK→CLASS)CLASS(class, leader)ACTIVITY(aid, activity)PARTICIPATION(sid FK→STUDENT, aid FK→ACTIVITY, hours)
BCNF ✓
Unchanged from 3NF

Every determinant shown is a key of its own relation.

Dependency-to-table reasoning

  • The original display is not 1NF because aid/activity/hours contain lists. Explode into one row per student–activity.
  • Key is (sid,aid). Dependencies on sid and aid alone violate 2NF, so separate Student and Activity facts.
  • class→leader makes leader transitively dependent on sid, so separate Class.
  • hours describes one student in one activity and stays in the bridge.
Decomposition check Every source attribute appears; all source facts can be reconstructed with joins; no table stores the same semantic fact twice; every non-trivial determinant in each result is a key.

Normalize by determinant: student facts→STUDENT, activity facts→ACTIVITY, class facts→CLASS, pair facts→bridge(sid,aid,…).

Additional Exercises 2–3 · ec_order to 3NF

corrected against 1,280 source rows

Exam answer

customer_id→customer attributes; order_id→date, payment_id, customer_id; payment_id→card_number,payment_amount; item_id→name,unit_price; (order_id,item_id)→quantity.

Candidate key of the original 1NF relation: (order_id, item_id).

ALTER TABLE ec_order RENAME TO ec_order_old;

CREATE TABLE ec_customer (
  customer_id integer PRIMARY KEY, gender varchar(6),
  firstname varchar(50), lastname varchar(50), street varchar(75),
  house_number varchar(5), zip_code char(5), city varchar(75)
);
CREATE TABLE ec_order (
  order_id integer PRIMARY KEY, order_date date,
  customer_id integer NOT NULL REFERENCES ec_customer(customer_id)
);
CREATE TABLE ec_payment (
  payment_id bigint PRIMARY KEY, card_number varchar(20),
  payment_amount numeric(10,2), order_id integer NOT NULL UNIQUE
  REFERENCES ec_order(order_id)
);
CREATE TABLE ec_item (
  item_id integer PRIMARY KEY, item_name varchar(100),
  unit_price numeric(10,2)
);
CREATE TABLE ec_order_item (
  order_id integer REFERENCES ec_order(order_id),
  item_id integer REFERENCES ec_item(item_id),
  quantity integer NOT NULL CHECK (quantity > 0),
  PRIMARY KEY (order_id,item_id)
);

INSERT INTO ec_customer

  or_street,or_house_number,or_zip_code,or_city FROM ec_order_old;

FROM ec_order_old;

  CHECK (unit_price BETWEEN 0 AND 10000);

Classroom working example · build every stage

The FDs, candidate key, final five-table DDL, and data-copy statements above remain the original answer. This example shows the intermediate normal-form schemas.

1NF ✓
Atomic wide order-line relation

One row per (order_id, item_id); all cells are atomic.

order_id-only and item_id-only facts are partial dependencies ↓
2NF ✓
Separate order, item, and pair facts
ORDER_2NF(order_id, date, payment_id, card_number, payment_amount, customer_id, customer attributes)ITEM(item_id, name, unit_price)ORDER_ITEM(order_id, item_id, quantity)
customer_id and payment_id determine non-key details inside ORDER_2NF ↓
3NF ✓
Split the transitive customer and payment facts
CUSTOMER(customer_id, customer attributes)ORDER(order_id, date, customer_id FK)PAYMENT(payment_id, card_number, payment_amount, order_id UNIQUE FK)ITEM(item_id, name, unit_price)ORDER_ITEM(order_id, item_id, quantity)

Each non-trivial determinant is a candidate key in its own relation; PAYMENT has candidate keys payment_id and order_id under the one-payment-per-order rule.

Corrections and verification

  • Quantity is not determined by item_id. It varies per order line; the correct FD is (order_id,item_id)→quantity. The supplied FD list places it under item_id.
  • City must be copied. The supplied customer INSERT selects seven values into an eight-column table and therefore fails; the corrected statement includes or_city.
  • Do not store both directions of the same 1:1 link. This design keeps order_id UNIQUE in Payment and omits duplicated payment_id from Order.
  • Verified cardinalities: 321 customers, 384 orders, 384 payments, 84 items, 1,280 order lines. No item ID maps to conflicting names/prices and no payment maps to multiple orders.
Copy-data recipe Rename source → create parent tables → INSERT DISTINCT parents → insert child/bridge tables → compare counts → add validated constraints → only then drop the old table.

Order-line FD: item_id→name,unit_price; (order_id,item_id)→quantity. Quantity belongs in ORDER_ITEM, not ITEM.

Learning Lab 07 abstract relation: the fast conclusion

R(A,B,C,D,E,F), F = {A→B, CD→A, BC→D, AE→F, CE→F}

machine-verified candidate keys

Exam answer

C and E never appear on a RHS, so every key contains CE. Closures show ACE, BCE, and CDE each determine all attributes; removing any attribute from each fails.

Candidate keys: ACE, BCE, CDE. Not BCNF: A→B has determinant A, which is not a superkey (and other violations can be shown similarly).

Caution

The supplied answer’s decomposition AB, BCD, AEF does not preserve every listed dependency (notably CD→A and CE→F) as local constraints. The task asks only for keys and the BCNF verdict. If a decomposition is explicitly requested, one verified lossless BCNF result is CEF, AB, ACD, CDE; it does not preserve BC→D and AE→F locally, illustrating the dependency-preservation trade-off.

Classroom status-ladder example

1NF is assumed. It is not in 2NF because CE→F makes non-prime F depend on a proper subset of every candidate key; therefore it is not in 3NF. It is not in BCNF because A→B has a determinant that is not a superkey. Highest normal form: 1NF.

Paper check Write the ladder 1NF → 2NF failure → 3NF failure → BCNF counterexample. One counterexample FD is enough for BCNF: name it and show its determinant’s closure is not all attributes.

BCNF proof of failure: exhibit one non-trivial X→Y with X⁺ ≠ all attributes; decompose only if asked, then check losslessness and dependency preservation separately.

4

Relational algebra: construct the result set

Read an expression from the inside out; write one operator for each phrase in the question.

🔴 Exam-core Prof. Scholz explicitly named Relational Algebra as a focus on 22 July 2026; the final-exam slide, Homework 05, and Learning Lab 06 corroborate it.

Operator vocabulary

OperatorMeaningSchema/result warning
σcondition(R)Select rows.Schema unchanged.
πattributes(R)Project columns.Relational algebra removes duplicates.
ρalias(R)Rename relation/attributes.Needed for self-joins and ambiguous names.
R ∪ S, R ∩ S, R − SSet combine/compare.R and S must be union-compatible: same arity and matching domains.
R × SEvery pair.Usually an intermediate before selection; size |R|×|S|.
R ⋈θ SJoin matching pairs by explicit condition.Safest when names overlap.
R ⋈ SNatural join on all same-named attributes.Convenient only when every same name is intended as a join key.
Natural-join trapIf two relations both contain name or semester, natural join uses all such equal-name columns. Rename first or use a theta join so the predicate is visible.

complete trace

Exam answer

σName='Konstantin Pfeiffer'(Professor) → professor #004. Project Professor# → {004}. Join with TakesPlace on Professor# → lecture 002 WT2023 and lecture 003 WT2023.

WeekdayTimeslot

Procedure

Start at leaves, write each intermediate schema as well as rows. A projection node can discard a future join key only if the join has already used it.

Paper recipe Under each tree node write schema: … and then its rows. If a column needed by the parent disappeared, your projection is too early.

Operation tree: evaluate bottom-up; record schema at every node; never project away a key needed above.
